Non-Chord Tones: Practice for Chapter 10

Exercises for Chapter 10 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom: passing and neighbor tones, appoggiaturas, escape tones, double neighbors, anticipations, pedal points, suspensions and retardations, with the book’s listening examples.

This page goes with Chapter 10, Non-Chord Tones of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It builds on Chapter 6, Triads and Chapter 9, Harmonic Progression.

How the drills work: each one shows two bars of melody over chords (the chords are also in the bass clef) and plays them. One note of the melody is marked *: it is not in the chord under it. Name it with the buttons or a key (shown under each drill). After you answer, the drill says whether it was accented and how it was approached and left. Each section adds the new type to the ones before. Every drill has Settings (keys, minor, hiding the chord symbols), and is also on the Theory Drills page.

10.1 What a non-chord tone is

A non-chord tone (also called an embellishing or non-harmonic tone) is a note that is not part of the chord sounding with it. The book names nine kinds, told apart by how the note is approached and how it is left: by the same note, by a step, or by a leap.

Non-chord tone Approached by Left by
Passing tone step step in the same direction
Neighbor tone step step in the opposite direction (back to the first note)
Appoggiatura leap step
Escape tone step leap in the opposite direction
Double neighbor step two non-chord tones, one each side of a chord tone, then back to it
Anticipation step the same note (it arrives early, before its chord)
Pedal point the same note the same note (held while the chords change)
Suspension the same note step down
Retardation the same note step up

Words that can go in front of any of them: accented (on the beat) or unaccented (off the beat); chromatic (outside the key); and metrical, sub-metrical or super-metrical (as long as a beat, shorter, longer). Read 10.1 · Open Music Theory: Embellishing Tones

Learn the table first. This is the book’s exercise 1, as a drill:

To find one in music: name the chord, then go through the melody note by note asking “is this in the chord?” For each note that is not, look at the note before and the note after.

10.2 Passing tones

A passing tone fills the gap between two chord tones a third apart, moving by step in one direction. Two passing tones in a row can fill a fourth (from the root down to the fifth, say). Most are unaccented; an accented one lands on the beat and moves on to the chord tone. Read 10.2

10.3 Neighbor tones

A neighbor tone steps away from a chord tone and steps straight back to it: an upper neighbor above, a lower neighbor below. Read 10.3

10.4 Appoggiatura

An appoggiatura is reached by a leap and left by a step. It is usually on the beat, which is what makes it so expressive: the dissonance is the strong note and the resolution the weak one. The leap and the step can go either way; the drills use the most common shape, the step going back against the leap. Read 10.4

10.5 Escape tone

An escape tone is the appoggiatura turned around: a step away from a chord tone, then a leap the other way. It is usually unaccented. The word “of” in “home of the brave”, at the end of “The Star-Spangled Banner”, is one. Read 10.5

10.6 Double neighbor

A double neighbor (or neighbor group) visits both neighbors, upper and lower in either order, before returning to the chord tone. Two non-chord tones in a row, so it is easy to mistake for an escape tone followed by an appoggiatura: keep track of which notes are in the chord. (The drills mark both notes.) Read 10.6

10.7 Anticipation

An anticipation sounds a note of the next chord just before that chord arrives, so it is heard twice: early (a non-chord tone) and on time (a chord tone). It is common at cadences, and syncopated pop melodies are full of them. Read 10.7

10.8 Pedal point

A pedal point is a note held (or repeated) while the chords change around it. It starts as a chord tone, becomes a non-chord tone when the harmony moves away, and usually ends as a chord tone again. Pedals are most often in the bass (the name comes from the organ’s foot pedals), where they make the chord’s inversion not worth naming; they can also be in an upper voice, as in the drills, or two at once (a double pedal, often a fifth apart). Read 10.8

10.9 Suspension

A suspension holds a note over from one chord into the next, where it no longer fits, then resolves down by step. It has three parts: the preparation (a chord tone), the suspension (the same note, now dissonant, on the beat) and the resolution. The preparation is often tied to the suspension.

Suspensions are named by two intervals above the bass: the suspended note, then its resolution, with compound intervals reduced: 4-3, 7-6, 9-8 (kept as 9, not 2), 6-5, and 2-3, the bass suspension, measured from the bass up to an upper voice. With an inverted chord you will meet other numbers (5-4, 3-2). The drill’s feedback names the figure. Read 10.9 · Open Music Theory: Embellishing Tones

10.10 Retardation

A retardation is a suspension that resolves up by step. Like a suspension it is held over and usually on the beat. Classical composers liked both at cadences in slow movements. Read 10.10

10.11 Incomplete neighbor

Real music does not always fit the table. A note may have two good explanations, or none. The book’s catch-all is the incomplete neighbor: a neighbor tone with one side missing. Keep an open mind, and say what you hear. (It is not in the drills, because the book leaves it loosely defined.) Read 10.11

10.12 Everything together

All nine kinds, major and minor. Set Questions to 20 for a score. Practice exercises with answers (10.12)

Harder: the chord symbols are hidden, so you read each chord from the bass clef first, as you would in a score.

For teachers
  • Links with your settings: open a drill’s Settings, then Copy a link with these settings. Add &lock=1 for a test, &count=20 for a score. For example theory-drills.html?ex=nct&types=SUS,RET&mode=both&count=20.
  • What the drills write: two bars of 4/4, a melody over three chords (two in the first bar, one in the second) taken from short diatonic progressions (I–V–I, ii–V–I, I–vi–V, i–iv–i, …), with the chords as close triads in the bass clef. Every melody note is a chord tone except the marked one (two for a double neighbor). Unaccented tones are eighth notes off the beat; accented ones fall on beat 1 or 3 (a double neighbor is two quarter notes, beats 2 and 3). Pedal points are a held tonic in the melody over I–IV–V–I (or I–vi–V–I, i–iv–V–i).
  • Not drilled: chromatic non-chord tones (the melodies stay in the key; in minor, the leading tone is raised only over V), appoggiaturas whose step goes the same way as the leap, incomplete neighbors, and bass pedals and bass (2-3) suspensions. The text covers them.
  • Checked: node tests/lessons/nct-drill.test.js generates 7,200 questions and has the site’s separate non-chord-tone analyser (abc-nht.js) confirm that each marked note is the type asked and every other note a chord tone.
  • Videos: the clips use the book’s YouTube links and start and end times; each title was checked against YouTube.
